title: The Cognitive Revolution and Cave Art

cards.h: Why would someone crawl into a dark cave to paint a bull?
cards.b:
About 40,000 years ago, people started leaving marks that said 'we were here, and we thought about things'. Painted animals, carved figures, flutes made of bone.

Something in the human mind lit up. Let us visit the oldest art galleries on Earth.

cards.h: The oldest paintings keep getting older
cards.b:
In Indonesia's Sulawesi island, a painted pig has been dated to at least 45,500 years ago, and hand stencils to about 40,000. Some Sulawesi art has now been dated even older, by dating the thin mineral crust over it.

The oldest known art keeps moving back as dating improves. That is why you should treat 'oldest' claims as 'oldest so far'.

cards.h: The cave that was a time capsule
cards.b:
In 1994, three explorers found Chauvet Cave in southern France. It had been sealed by a rockfall for about 20,000 years. Inside: lions, rhinos, horses and bears painted about 30,000-36,000 years ago.

Later, Lascaux (France, about 17,000 years old) was found by teenagers chasing a dog, in 1940. Its bulls are huge and gorgeous.

The Lion-man of the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany is a carved ivory figure with a human body and a lion's head. It is about 40,000 years old. It shows people could imagine things that do not exist. Some scholars link this to early belief or stories.

cards.h: What was going on in their heads?
cards.b:
Historians call this the Cognitive Revolution, a term popularised by Yuval Noah Harari. The big idea: humans got better at language, planning and imagination.

But this idea is debated. Some archaeologists think there was no sudden 'revolution'. Neanderthals may have made art too: engravings and painted shells in Spain are claimed to be Neanderthal, though the dating is contested.

Bone flutes made from vulture bone and mammoth ivory from caves in Germany are about 40,000 years old. Shell beads travelled hundreds of kilometres. That tells us about trade and identity.

Somebody wore beads to say who they were.

Myth: cave people were dim.Fact: their brains were the same size as ours. The artists used shading, perspective and clever use of rock bumps to make animals look alive.

Something else: nobody knows why they painted. 'Hunting magic', shamans in trances and storytelling are all guesses. Historians argue and none of the guesses is proven.

Bhimbetka and the painted shelters

At Bhimbetka, near Bhopal, about 750 rock shelters hold thousands of paintings, in red from haematite and in white. They show bison, deer, hunters with bows, dancers and riders. V. S. Wakankar spotted the site from a train in 1957. UNESCO listed it in 2003.

Most of the paintings come from the Mesolithic, about 10,000 years ago, and some were added much later. The oldest marks are cup-shaped hollows (cupules) that may be far older, though their dating is still argued.

The Cognitive Revolution is usually told through Lascaux and Chauvet. Bhimbetka shows that people in central India were also painting their imagination on stone.

Five things to remember

  1. Art and symbols appear at least 45,000 years ago.
  2. Chauvet and Lascaux are famous cave galleries in France.
  3. The Lion-man shows imagination of unreal beings.
  4. Whether it was a sudden 'revolution' is debated.
  5. Bhimbetka shows India's long rock art tradition.

Think about it

  • Why might people paint deep in dark caves rather than outside?
  • If Neanderthals made art, what changes in the story?
